# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–25 (Complete – Updated 178)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of seventh year** (Chapter 25). Major Dobbin has arrived in England and reunited with Amelia. Rawdon governs Coventry Island (winter of sixth year). Georgy established at Russell Square with grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 24 opened "winter of sixth year"; Chapter 25 opens "spring of seventh year."
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe hill farms; Bryngate market town; Piccadilly; Madras (India); St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; various English countryside towns.

## The Duel Resolution and Its Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23–24)

**Macmurdo's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: When Rawdon wavered after learning of Coventry Island appointment, Macmurdo rebuked him, insisting affair was placed in his hands. Refused to carry further challenge; argued duel would disgrace all parties. Advised Rawdon to accept position and maintain silence.

**Duel Occurred (Chapter 24)**: Secret rencontre between Rawdon and Steyne; principals and seconds agreed to bury outcome "in the profoundest oblivion." Despite sworn secrecy, story spread rapidly across London within hours. **Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Mr. Wagg acting on Wenham's hint**—kept from press.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation (Chapter 24)**: Rawdon refused Pitt's reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money from him ten years; she swore she had none from Steyne, but "directly I found it" she knew "it was all up." Rawdon declared: "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty, and I'll never see her again--never."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship (Chapter 24)**: Initially resisted appointment "procured for him by so odious a patron" (Steyne). Persuaded to accept by Pitt's entreaties and mainly Macmurdo's argument that accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Final Dissolution (Chapter 24)

**Household Seized**: Bailiffs seized Raggles's property in Curzon Street. Rebecca's fate immediately after unknown—"where? Who cared!"

**Financial Arrangements**: Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity"—she possessed talent for "making a little money go a great way."

## Rawdon's Life in Coventry Island (Chapter 24)

**Colonial Governance**: Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand a year. Maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education and future, compensates those wronged (Briggs via Pitt). Complete moral transformation accomplished.

## Georgy Osborne's Establishment and Education (Chapter 24)

**Current Status**: "Fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square, occupant of his father's room...and heir apparent of all the splendours there." Mr. Osborne "as proud of him as ever he had been of the elder George"—boy's "good looks, gallant bearing, and gentlemanlike appearance" won grandsire's heart.

**Intellectual Superiority**: Georgy's superior education made him "a much better gentleman" than grandfather's plans. Boy's "quick brain and better education" showed grandfather was "a dullard." Boy began "accordingly to command him and to look down upon him."

**Physical Appearance and Dress**: Scarcely eleven years old; wore straps, beautiful little boots, gilt spurs, gold-headed whip. Dressed for dinner daily "like a regular West End swell." One domestic specially attended him.

**Daily Habits**: After breakfast, sat reading Morning Post "just like a grown-up man." Made house lively "by his activity, his imperiousness, his scolding, and his good-nature." Domineer[s] over everybody; "in Russell Square, everybody was afraid of Mr. Osborne, and Mr. Osborne was afraid of Georgy."

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Master George's great friend. Both attended principal theatres; knew names of all actors. **Mrs. Todd's private plan (rumor)**: Noted Georgy and her youngest daughter Rosa Jemima "looked so well together" and privately wondered "who knows what might happen?"

**Reverend Lawrence Veal's School** (Hart Street, Bloomsbury): Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Georgy is day boy only, arrives mornings under Rowson's guardianship, rides away afternoons on pony. **Notable failing**: Veal frequently tolerates Georgy's late arrival and defaulting behavior without consequences. Marked: aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French.

**Amelia's Involvement with School**: Made friends with Mrs. Veal "for reasons of her own." Attended Mrs. Veal's monthly conversazioni with pink cards. Walked from Brompton "in any weather" and embraced Mrs. Veal "with tearful gratitude."

**Emotional Indifference**: Georgy bears separation from Amelia easily, whilst "his mother was yearning after him at home...every hour of the day."

## Amelia's Captivity and Suffering (Chapter 24)

**Mrs. Sedley's Death**: Few months after Georgy began with paternal grandfather, Mrs. Sedley died. "There had been little love between her and the child. He did not care to show much grief. He came down to visit his mother in a fine new suit of mourning, and was very angry that he could not go to a play." Amelia had smoothed pillow; soothed sufferer with words of hope; "closed the eyes that had once looked so tenderly upon her."

**John Sedley's Destitution**: Old man "stunned by the blow which had befallen him." "There was only Amelia to stand by and support with her gentle arms the tottering, heart-broken old man."

**Financial Dependence on Osborne**: "One of the many causes for personal pride with which old Osborne chose to recreate himself that Sedley...was in his last days so utterly defeated and humiliated as to be forced to accept pecuniary obligations at the hands of the man who had most injured and insulted him." Osborne "cursed the old pauper and relieved him from time to time."

**Amelia's Acceptance and Prison**: Her life "had come down to this--to a mean prison and a long, ignoble bondage." Russell Square was "the boundary of her prison: she might walk thither occasionally, but was always back to sleep in her cell at night."

**Amelia's Devotion**: She determined "with all her might and strength to try and make her old father happy. She slaved, toiled, patched, and mended, sang and played backgammon, read out the newspaper, cooked dishes for old Sedley, walked him out sedulously into Kensington Gardens or the Brompton Lanes, listened to his stories with untiring smiles and affectionate hypocrisy."

**Miniature Portrait**: Georgy commissioned miniature of himself, paying from own money. Old Osborne, pleased, gave boy twice the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung portrait beside another miniature (George's) over her bed. Slept with picture under pillow; kissed and wept and prayed over it "many many times." "Since her parting with George she had had no such joy and consolation."

## Major Dobbin's Return and First Reunion (Chapter 24–25)

**Illness in Madras**: Major Dobbin obtained leave, travelled "night and day until he reached his journey's end." Arrived at Madras "in a high fever." Servants brought him to friend's house "in a state of delirium"; thought for many days he would not travel farther than "the burying-ground of the church of St. George's."

**Delirium and Testament**: During fever, "the poor fellow lay tossing in his fever...raving about Amelia." Made solemn preparations, leaving "the little property of which he was possessed to those whom he most desired to benefit." Wore "a little brown hair-chain which he...had got from Amelia's maid at Brussels...when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne on the plateau at Mount St. John."

**Recovery and Passage on Ramchunder**: Dobbin recovered and took passage with Jos Sedley. After passing St. Helena, displayed "gaiety and strength" astonishing to fellow passengers. Became "so impatient and ill-humoured" within ten days' sail of England, recovered when breeze sprang up. "Good God, how his heart beat as the two friendly spires of Southampton came in sight."

**Landing and Journey Inland**: Entire crew gave three cheers for Major Dobbin at landing. Jos, "who very likely thought the cheers were for himself, took off his gold-laced cap and waved it majestically." They proceeded to Royal George Hotel. Dobbin made early departure next morning, "obliged to retreat, leaving Jos to resume his interrupted slumbers."

**Rapid Journey to London**: Travelled rapidly "as if he had been an English nobleman travelling on a pleasure tour." Post-boys wondered at fees. At Slaughters' Inn, inquired about "Captain Osborne's widow"; innkeeper John noted loan from April 1815. Dobbin "chose out of his kit the very smartest and most becoming civil costume he possessed, and laughed at his own tanned face and grey hair."

**Reunion with Clapps and Binny (Chapter 25)**: Dobbin called at Clapp's house in Brompton. Was greeted by Miss Mary Polly Clapp. Identified himself as "an old friend," Georgy's godfather, "just come back from India." **Reverend Mr. Binny's Marriage**: Dobbin learned from Miss Clapp that Reverend Binny had married Miss Grits (grocer's daughter, five thousand pound fortune) and just returned from Margate. Dobbin's "head was swimming with felicity"—he had no longer a rival to fear.

**Meeting with Amelia (Chapter 25)**: "Old Sedley was seated on a bench, his handkerchief placed over his knees, prattling away, according to his wont, with some old story about old times." When Mary appeared, "Amelia caught sight of her, she started up from her bench. Her first thought was that something had happened to Georgy, but the sight of the messenger's eager and happy face dissipated that fear." Dobbin's "lean figure and long shadow stalking across the grass" caused Amelia to start, blush, and cry. She came "running towards him, her hands before her, ready to give them to him." "She wasn't changed. She was a little pale, a little stouter in figure. Her eyes were the same, the kind trustful eyes. There were scarce three lines of silver in her soft brown hair." He took "the two little hands between his two and held them there. He was speechless for a moment. Why did he not take her in his arms and swear that he would never leave her? She must have yielded: she could not but have obeyed him."

**Internal Conflict (Chapter 25)**: As holding Amelia's hand, "Ought I to be angry with her for being faithful to him?...Ought I to be jealous of my friend in the grave, or hurt that such a heart as Amelia's can love only once and for ever? Oh, George, George, how little you knew the prize you had, though."

**Tea at Sedley's Home (Chapter 25)**: Although "he had such particular business in London that evening," Dobbin consented to forego it upon Mr. Sedley's invitation to tea. "Amelia put her arm under that of her young friend with the yellow shawl and headed the party on their return homewards, so that Mr. Sedley fell to Dobbin's share." Old man "walked very slowly and told a number of ancient histories about himself and his poor Bessy, his former prosperity, and his bankruptcy." Dobbin's "eyes were fixed upon the figure in front of him--the dear little figure always present to his imagination and in his prayers, and visiting his dreams wakeful or slumbering."

**Amelia's Hospitality (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia was very happy, smiling, and active all that evening, performing her duties as hostess of the little entertainment with the utmost grace and propriety, as Dobbin thought. His eyes followed her about as they sat in the twilight." He had "longed for that moment and thought of her far away under hot winds and in weary marches, gentle and happy, kindly ministering to the wants of old age, and decorating poverty with sweet submission--as he saw her now."

**Amelia Encourages Tea (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia seeing this propensity, laughingly encouraged it and looked exceedingly roguish as she administered to him cup after cup." She did not know "that the Major had had no dinner and that the cloth was laid for him at the Slaughters', and a plate laid thereon to mark that the table was retained, in that very box in which the Major and George had sat many a time carousing, when she was a child just come home from Miss Pinkerton's school."

**Dobbin's Hesitation and Departure (Chapter 25)**: When pressed to stay "to-morrow," Dobbin demurred: "Not to-morrow...I have business." He did not like to own "that he had not as yet been to his parents' and his dear sister Anne--a remissness for which I am sure every well-regulated person will blame the Major." He took his leave, leaving his address for Jos. "And so the first day was over, and he had seen her. When he got back to the Slaughters', the roast fowl was of course cold, in which condition he ate it for supper...Major Dobbin treated himself to half-price at the Haymarket Theatre that evening, where let us hope he enjoyed himself."

## Jos Sedley's Return (Chapter 25)

**Ten Years in Bengal**: Jos had passed ten years in Bengal. "Constant dinners, tiffins, pale ale and claret, the prodigious labour of cutcherry, and the refreshment of brandy-pawnee which he was forced to take there, had their effect upon Waterloo Sedley." Served full time with fine appointments, laid by considerable money, returned to Europe with good pension.

**Passage on Ramchunder**: After leaving St. Helena, became "very generous, disposing of a great quantity of ship stores." No ladies on board; Jos was "the first dignitary at table." Disappeared "rather in a panic during a two-days' gale," remained in cot reading *The Washerwoman of Finchley Common*. Many nights "the ship was cutting through the roaring dark sea...Mr. Sedley and the Major would sit on the quarter-deck of the vessel talking about home, as the Major smoked his cheroot."

**Dobbin's Persuasion**: Dobbin "rightly suspected that his travelling companion never would be got into motion in so short a space as twenty-four hours, and would find some excuse for delaying." The Major "had impressed this duty most strongly upon his fellow-passenger and extorted promises from him that he would take charge of his sister and her child."

**Jos's Delay and Letter (Chapter 25)**: Jos sent letter from Southampton announcing he felt fatigued after voyage and could not move that day, but would leave early next morning and arrive at evening. **Dobbin had not written to Jos to inform him of Mrs. Sedley's death**, being occupied in talking with Amelia until long after post-hour. Jos spent time hiring servant, instructing agent, and having waistcoats made.

**Reunion with Father and Sister (Chapter 25)**: Upon arrival, "All the faces in the street were in the windows; the little maidservant flew to the wicket-gate; the Mesdames Clapp looked out from the casement of the ornamented kitchen; Emmy, in a great flutter, was in the passage among the hats and coats; and old Sedley in the parlour inside, shaking all over." Jos descended "in awful state, supported by the new valet from Southampton and the shuddering native, whose brown face was now livid with cold and of the colour of a turkey's gizzard." Emmy warned him not to speak of mother's death to their father; but old Sedley "began immediately to speak of the event, and prattled about it, and wept over it plenteously."

**Jos's Declaration (Chapter 25)**: Jos declared "that they should never suffer want or discomfort any more, that he was at home for some time at any rate, during which his house and everything he had should be theirs: and that Amelia would look very pretty at the head of his table--until she would accept one of her own."

## Amelia's Response to Dobbin's Presence and Feelings (Chapter 25)

**Awareness without Rebuff (Chapter 25)**: "Not that Emmy, being made aware of the honest Major's passion, rebuffed him in any way, or felt displeased with him. Such an attachment from so true and loyal a gentleman could make no woman angry." She would give him "that friendly regard, which so much excellence and fidelity merited; she would treat him with perfect cordiality and frankness until he made his proposals, and THEN it would be time enough for her to speak and to put an end to hopes which never could be realized."

**Reaction to Jos's Hint (Chapter 25)**: When Jos hinted at her remarrying, "She shook her head sadly and had, as usual, recourse to the waterworks."

**Polly's Observations and Confidences (Chapter 25)**: "She and her young confidante, Miss Mary, had talked over the matter most fully, the very night of the Major's visit, beyond which time the impetuous Polly could not refrain from talking of the discovery which she had made, and describing the start and tremor of joy by which Major Dobbin betrayed himself when Mr. Binny passed with his bride and the Major learned that he had no longer a rival to fear." Polly noted Dobbin "shook all over" when learning of Binny's marriage, saying "he never kept his eyes off you, and I'm sure he's grown grey athinking of you."

**Amelia's Steadfast Refusal (Chapter 25)**: Amelia told Polly "never, never, to speak on that subject again; that Major Dobbin had been her husband's dearest friend and her own and George's most kind and affectionate guardian; that she loved him as a brother--but that a woman who had been married to such an angel as that, and she pointed to the wall, could never think of any other union." After conversation with Polly, "She slept, therefore, very soundly that evening...and was more than ordinarily happy." She thought: "I am glad he is not going to marry that Miss O'Dowd. Colonel O'Dowd never could have a sister fit for such an accomplished man as Major William." She imagined finding him a wife but "could not find anybody to suit the Major before she went to sleep."

## Amelia's Move from Brompton (Chapter 25)

**Separation from Mary Clapp**: "As for Miss Mary, her sorrow at Amelia's departure was such as I shall not attempt to depict. From childhood upwards she had been with her daily and had attached herself so passionately to that dear good lady that when the grand barouche came to carry her off into splendour, she fainted in the arms of her friend, who was indeed scarcely less affected than the good-natured girl. Amelia loved her like a daughter. During eleven years the girl had been her constant friend and associate." It was arranged Mary would visit the grand new house, though "Poor Emmy's days of happiness had been very few in that humble cot. A gloomy Fate had oppressed her there." She remembered "the landlady who had tyrannized over her when ill-humoured and unpaid" and her "coarse sycophant" manner when Emmy later prospered.

**Mary Clapp's Romance (Rumor)**: "I may mention that poor Mary, when left at her friend's departure in a hysterical condition, was placed under the medical treatment of the young fellow from the surgery, under whose care she rallied after a short period."

**Transfer of Furnishings**: Emmy "endowed Mary with every article of furniture that the house contained, only taking away her pictures (the two pictures over the bed) and her piano--that little old piano which had now passed into a plaintive jingling old age, but which she loved for reasons of her own. She was a child when first she played on it, and her parents gave it her. It had been given to her again since, as the reader may remember, when her father's house was gone to ruin and the instrument was recovered out of the wreck."

## Piano Discovery and Amelia's Disillusionment (Chapter 25)

**Dobbin's Subtle Role**: Major Dobbin "was exceedingly pleased when, as he was superintending the arrangements of Jos's new house...the cart arrived from Brompton, bringing the trunks and bandboxes of the emigrants from that village, and with them the old piano. Amelia would have it up in her sitting-room, a neat little apartment on the second floor, adjoining her father's chamber."

**The Revealing Question (Chapter 25)**: "Do you, Amelia?" cried the Major when she expressed appreciation for the piano. Dobbin, who had secretly purchased it, "never said anything about it, it never entered into his head to suppose that Emmy should think anybody else was the purchaser, and as a matter of course he fancied that she knew the gift came from him." But his question revealed his expectation, and "the question, the great question of all, was trembling on his lips, when Emmy replied--"

**Amelia's Realization and Pain (Chapter 25)**: "Emmy did not note the circumstance at the time, nor take immediate heed of the very dismal expression which honest Dobbin's countenance assumed, but she thought of it afterwards. And then it struck her, with inexpressible pain and mortification too, that it was William who was the giver of the piano, and not George, as she had fancied. It was not George's gift; the only one which she had received from her lover, as she thought--the thing she had cherished beyond all others--her dearest relic and prize. She had spoken to it about George; played his favourite airs upon it; sat for long evening hours, touching, to the best of her simple art, melancholy harmonies on the keys, and weeping over them in silence. It was not George's relic. It was valueless now. The next time that old Sedley asked her to play, she said it was shockingly out of tune, that she had a headache, that she couldn't play."

**Attempted Reparation (Chapter 25)**: "Then, according to her custom, she rebuked herself for her pettishness and ingratitude and determined to make a reparation to honest William for the slight she had not expressed to him, but had felt for his piano. A few days afterwards, as they were seated in the drawing-room, where Jos had fallen asleep with great comfort after dinner, Amelia said with rather a faltering voice to Major Dobbin--" [Text cut off; moment incomplete.]
